title: How must Ruhee join two strips to get a rectangle?
description: A workshop is full of wooden frames, some neat and some leaning, and each has four straight sides. Ruhee crosses two thin strips and passes a thread through their ends, and the video stops on how to join them for an exact rectangle.
teaching_notes: One idea: four sided shapes are everywhere, and making one that is exactly a rectangle needs a sure method. Watch for students who think any two strips will do because the thread always makes four sides.

source: What makes a figure a quadrilateral?
video_script.why: Before any property appears, the child meets the problem that drives the chapter: making a frame that is surely a rectangle.
video_script.substitution: Two thin wooden strips crossed on a workbench, with a thread passed through their four ends.
video_script.anchor: a wooden frame workshop, with two thin strips crossed on the workbench and a thread through their ends

names.Ruhee: the carpenter who joins two wooden strips so that a thread through their ends makes a rectangle

hold_back: the strips must cross at their midpoints
never_show: any answer to how the strips are joined
maths_rules: The frames in the workshop are closed shapes with four straight sides; some are neat, some lean, one caves in at a corner.
Two strips cross; a thread through their four ends makes a four sided shape.
No length, angle or number is drawn or said; nothing is measured.
The open question: how must the strips be joined so the thread makes an exact rectangle. It is never answered here.
video_script.design: One idea: a sure way to make an exact rectangle is needed. Assumes nothing. The workshop stays to the end and the question is never answered.
